items.title: Kosher rules separate meat and dairy
items.claim: What are the main categories of kosher (kashrut) restrictions?

options.text: Permitted animals (mammals that chew cud and have cloven hooves; fish with fins and scales); ritual slaughter (shechita); separation of meat and dairy in cooking, eating and utensils; specific prohibitions including pork, shellfish, mixing milk and meat
Only meals at synagogue must be kosher

items.reveal:
The meat-dairy separation derives from three repetitions of 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). Rabbinic interpretation extended this to all mixing of meat and dairy.

Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 list permitted and forbidden animals. Pork and shellfish are the most widely known prohibitions; rabbit, camel and birds of prey are also forbidden.

Shechita is ritual slaughter by a trained shochet with a perfectly sharp knife in a single cut — designed to be quick and to drain blood. Some European countries (Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Belgian regions) have banned shechita without prior stunning on animal welfare grounds.
items.why: Religious practice is often embodied — daily eating, household kitchens, separate dishes. Kashrut is one of the clearest cases of belief expressed through bodily and domestic practice.

items.title: Varna (theory) and jati (lived caste) are not identical
items.claim: What is the relationship between varna and jati?

options.text: Varna is the fourfold theoretical division (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) described in the Vedas and Manusmriti; jati is the thousands of birth-based occupational groupings that form the lived caste system; Dalits ('untouchables') were outside the four varnas
Caste is purely social with no religious dimension
Caste was invented by British colonisers

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta (10.90) describes the four varnas emerging from a cosmic being. The Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) codifies caste duties.

B. R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), Dalit leader and chief architect of India's constitution, converted to Buddhism in 1956 with around 500,000 followers, partly to escape caste. The Indian Constitution (1950) outlaws untouchability.

The relationship between varna theory and the thousands of jatis on the ground is complex and historically contested. Caste discrimination persists in many forms; the UK Equality Act 2010 includes caste under race discrimination provisions.
items.why: Religious texts and social systems interact in ways that resist clean separation. The caste case shows how a tradition can be deployed for social hierarchy and also generate its own critics.
